question: When can rich feature learning generalize worse than lazy kernel training, and can the gap be explained by feature-regime sparsification making a predictor insufficiently smooth along task-invariant directions?

key_findings.claim: For one-hidden-layer ReLU interpolation on a sphere, the paper contrasts an atomic variation-norm solution as its feature regime with minimum-norm NTK or random-feature kernel interpolants as lazy regimes.
key_findings.evidence: The feature model minimizes total variation of a signed measure over neuron directions subject to fitting n observations; under a uniqueness assumption, a representer theorem gives at most n atoms. The lazy models instead interpolate with the analytical NTK or RFK. Small initialization without explicit regularization is empirically observed to yield O(n) feature groups as well, though not the same minimum-norm solution.

key_findings.claim: The central prediction is that sufficiently smooth isotropic targets are learned with a better sample-size exponent by lazy kernels than by sparse feature learning.
key_findings.evidence: For target spectral smoothness nu_t on S^{d-1}, the proposed exponents are beta_lazy=min{2(d-1)+4nu,2nu_t}/(d-1), with nu=1/2 for NTK and 3/2 for RFK, and beta_feature=min{(d-1)+3,2nu_t}/(d-1). Thus the target spectrum controls rough tasks, while the smoother kernel spectrum wins once target smoothness stops being the bottleneck.

key_findings.claim: The high-dimensional learning-curve formula is an asymptotic ansatz rather than a general theorem.
key_findings.evidence: The authors explicitly state that no general rigorous framework exists for ridgeless learning curves. They prove a more limited two-dimensional regularity statement for the interpolant, use a simplified one-singularity calculation to obtain scaling on the circle, then extrapolate to arbitrary dimension by assuming low modes match and high-mode phases decorrelate. Numerical experiments support but do not convert this extrapolation into a proof.

anchors.section: Decay of the error in d=2 and generalization to higher dimensions

key_findings.claim: Numerical sphere experiments reproduce the predicted separation for constant and smooth Gaussian targets, while revealing difficult optimization in the rich minimum-norm problem.
key_findings.evidence: The constant-target curves for dimensions 2, 3, and 5 and the varying-smoothness curves in dimension 5 follow the predicted slopes over the displayed ranges. The appendix reports that exact minimal-L1 convergence becomes computationally infeasible as n grows; test error plateaus before parameters converge, and small-initialization gradient descent reaches a different atomic solution whose O(n) support is enough for the same claimed exponent.

key_findings.claim: On three image datasets, wide fully connected networks trained in the lazy regime have both lower error and lower relative sensitivity to small diffeomorphisms than feature-regime counterparts.
key_findings.evidence: For MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, Figure 1 shows the analytical-NTK classifier below the H=1000 ensemble's test error as training-set size grows. Figure 6 shows smaller R_f, the ratio of response to maximum-entropy diffeomorphisms over response to norm-matched random perturbations, for lazy predictors. PCA plots also show feature directions clustering after rich training.

key_findings.claim: The image evidence is correlational: it is compatible with the sparsity-smoothness mechanism but does not isolate it from other differences between kernel and rich training.
key_findings.evidence: The experiments jointly change training dynamics, predictor class, implicit norm, optimization, and feature distribution. No intervention holds predictions or norms fixed while varying atom count, nor does the paper show that reducing sparsity alone restores diffeomorphism stability and accuracy. The conclusion therefore appropriately describes the finding as a plausible account and leaves modern convolutional feature learning unexplained.

method.core_idea: Compare the spectral smoothness of sparse variation-norm ReLU interpolants and fixed-kernel interpolants, then test whether the resulting smoothness gap appears along label-preserving transformations in images.
method.mechanism: Targets are isotropic Gaussian random fields on the unit sphere with spherical-harmonic coefficients decaying according to nu_t. Rich training is idealized as minimum total-variation interpolation over a signed measure of ReLU directions and, assuming a unique solution, has O(n) atoms. Lazy training is exact ridgeless regression with analytical NTK or RFK kernels. The authors use the high-frequency decay of the neuron or kernel spectrum, a rigorous circle regularity result, and a random-phase cutoff ansatz k_c proportional to n^{1/(d-1)} to predict learning-curve exponents. They then train wide fully connected image classifiers at small or large scale and compare accuracy, feature-direction clustering, and relative diffeomorphism sensitivity.
assumptions: Training inputs are noiseless, independent, and uniformly distributed on S^{d-1} for the theoretical task.

The target is an isotropic Gaussian random field with a prescribed power-law spherical-harmonic spectrum and almost all odd harmonics except degree one removed so a bias-free ReLU network can approximate it.
The variation-norm interpolation problem has a unique atomic minimizer with at most n atoms; genericity is argued but not proved for every sampled task.
For high-dimensional scaling, low spherical-harmonic modes are learned, high modes of the empirical density act as decorrelated Gaussian sums, and a single nearest-neighbor scale sets the cutoff.
Infinite-width feature behavior is adequately represented by width 1,000 plus ensemble averaging on the image benchmarks.
Relative sensitivity to the selected maximum-entropy diffeomorphism distribution is a meaningful proxy for a task-relevant invariance.
The absence of label noise, ridge regularization, augmentation, convolution, and pooling does not qualitatively change the mechanism under study.

techniques.role: Represents rich shallow-network training as minimum-L1 optimization over a signed neuron measure.
Provides exact infinite-width lazy comparators through analytical Gram matrices.
Relates target and predictor spectral decay to asymptotic sample-error exponents.
Tests whether small initialization or weight decay collapses a wide feature distribution into O(n) active groups.
Measures prediction change under smooth random image warps relative to norm-matched unstructured perturbations.
Checks global translations and boundary-pixel corruption to distinguish harmful from helpful learned invariances.

evaluations.setting: Constant-function interpolation on spheres with d=2, 3, and 5
evaluations.metric: Generalization error versus number of samples on log-log axes
evaluations.result: Feature and lazy curves follow the displayed predicted slopes; finite-time deviation remains for feature training at large n in d=2
evaluations.baseline: Analytical NTK regression versus minimum-L1 or small-initialization feature training

evaluations.setting: Gaussian random fields of varying smoothness on S^4
evaluations.metric: Learning-curve exponent beta and test-error decay
evaluations.result: Experiments support target-limited equality for rough fields and a lazy advantage for smoother fields
evaluations.baseline: Feature-regime ReLU interpolation versus NTK interpolation

evaluations.setting: MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 classification with fully connected networks
evaluations.metric: Test error versus training-set size, averaged over ten network/data initializations
evaluations.result: The analytical NTK lazy model consistently outperforms the width-1,000 feature-regime ensemble in the shown ranges
evaluations.baseline: Lazy analytical-NTK SVC versus small-initialization fully trained FCN

evaluations.setting: The same image predictors under small maximum-entropy diffeomorphisms
evaluations.metric: Relative sensitivity R_f normalized by equally sized random perturbations
evaluations.result: Lazy predictors have consistently lower R_f across datasets and sample sizes

evaluations.metric: Relative sensitivity to one-pixel translations and boundary-pixel noise
evaluations.result: Lazy training is smoother to translations, while feature learning is less sensitive to irrelevant boundary corruption
evaluations.baseline: Matched lazy and feature fully connected predictors

limitations: The headline high-dimensional exponents rely on a random-phase spectral ansatz; the formal proposition is a two-dimensional limit statement and does not establish Equation (3.4) for general d.

The rich comparator is a shallow bias-free ReLU variation-norm interpolant under a uniqueness/atomicity assumption, not a general account of depth, SGD, cross-entropy, normalization, residual connections, or attention.
The experiments are noiseless and ridgeless in the sphere setting, so the bias-variance tradeoff under label noise or regularization is not characterized.
Small-initialization gradient descent does not recover the minimum-variation solution in the appendix; agreement of an exponent does not establish equivalence of implicit biases.
Width 1,000 and finite ensembles approximate rather than realize the claimed infinite-width feature limit, and the approximation error is not bounded across n or datasets.
The image evidence links sparsity, R_f, and accuracy observationally but does not manipulate neuron-measure sparsity to demonstrate that it causes either loss of smoothness or excess error.
Relative sensitivity is a ratio: changes in the random-perturbation denominator can change R_f even when absolute diffeomorphism sensitivity is fixed.
The deformation family is hand-selected and only weakly label preserving; no per-example label validation or robustness to deformation magnitude is reported in the main comparison.

Classification comparisons focus on primitive fully connected networks without augmentation, while the motivating success of feature learning concerns architectures whose inductive biases are deliberately excluded.
The paper predicts asymptotic exponents but finite-data constants and crossover scales can dominate practical model selection, especially when the exponents are close.
failure_modes: A target is anisotropic or depends on a low-dimensional projection, so learned feature alignment overcomes the roughness cost and rich training wins, as prior theory predicts.
A convolutional or equivariant architecture represents the invariance compactly, invalidating the premise that a continuous distribution of fully connected neurons is needed.
Noisy labels make exact interpolation and high-frequency tail behavior dominated by noise rather than target smoothness.
Optimization stops before atomic features or the minimum-variation interpolant emerges, changing both support size and the measured learning curve.
The feature minimizer is nonunique, so different optimization paths select measures with different sparsity and smoothness.
A transformation changes the true class or the task relies on high-frequency deformation-sensitive cues, making low R_f harmful rather than beneficial.
The denominator of relative sensitivity shrinks under feature learning, exaggerating apparent deformation instability.
Finite width imposes its own approximation and variance errors, confounding a comparison stated in terms of infinite-width limits.
reusable_insights: Treat feature learning as a task-dependent bias, not an unconditional benefit: measure whether the target's invariances are sparse in the chosen architecture's feature dictionary.
When comparing rich and lazy regimes, report feature-support size, function-space smoothness, optimization convergence, and test error together rather than using parameter movement alone.
Use target families with controllable spectra to separate approximation smoothness from input dimension and to expose the crossover where predictor bias becomes limiting.
Normalize transformation sensitivity against generic perturbations, but also publish numerator and denominator separately to prevent ratio-only interpretations.
Establish causality by regularizing or resampling the neuron measure to vary atomicity while matching fit, norm, width, and optimization budget.
Audit whether an architectural invariance is cheaply representable: sparsity is beneficial for coordinate-selective structure but can be destructive for continuous group orbits.
Do not equate an empirical O(n) active-feature count with recovery of a specific convex minimum-norm solution.
open_questions: Can Equation (3.4) be proved for random samples in d>2 without the decorrelated-mode ansatz, including finite-n constants and concentration?
What replaces the atomicity story for deep convolutional networks whose learned channels may be sparse while spatial weight sharing represents continuous deformations?
Can a prospective diagnostic of target-orbit complexity predict before training whether rich or lazy scaling will be better?
Does explicit anti-sparsity or feature-distribution entropy regularization improve fully connected image models while preserving useful anisotropic feature selection?
How do label noise, ridge regularization, data augmentation, and early stopping alter the target-versus-predictor spectral crossover?
Can absolute diffeomorphism sensitivity, margins, and calibration mediate the accuracy gap after controlling for generic Jacobian norm?
Which implicit measure norm is selected by realistic optimizers at finite width, and when does it yield a unique atomic solution?

competitive_landscape.title: Kernel and Rich Regimes in Overparametrized Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Formalizes how initialization scale moves homogeneous models between kernel and rich implicit biases.
competitive_landscape.difference: It maps the regime transition and often emphasizes distinct rich biases; the reviewed paper asks when one rich bias, atomic shallow-ReLU interpolation, is worse because the target needs distributed smooth features.

competitive_landscape.title: Limitations of Lazy Training of Two-layers Neural Network
competitive_landscape.relationship: Exhibits tasks where fully trained two-layer networks outperform random-feature and neural-tangent models.
competitive_landscape.difference: It supplies the opposite side of the task-dependence tradeoff, using quadratic and Gaussian-mixture structure favorable to learned features; the reviewed work constructs smooth isotropic targets favorable to kernels.

competitive_landscape.title: When Do Neural Networks Outperform Kernel Methods?
competitive_landscape.relationship: Characterizes when feature learning exploits a low-dimensional target representation that isotropic kernels cannot efficiently recover.
competitive_landscape.difference: It focuses on benefits of anisotropic feature adaptation; the reviewed paper identifies the complementary failure case where forcing a sparse representation harms smooth invariant directions.

competitive_landscape.title: Relative Stability Toward Diffeomorphisms Indicates Performance in Deep Nets
competitive_landscape.relationship: Introduces the same maximum-entropy deformations and R_f statistic and reports its correlation with architecture performance.
competitive_landscape.difference: It establishes the diagnostic across modern networks; the reviewed paper uses it to propose a specific sparsification mechanism for the lazy-versus-feature gap in fully connected networks.

competitive_landscape.title: Benign Overfitting in Deep Neural Networks under Lazy Training
competitive_landscape.relationship: A later theory also connects smoother interpolating functions in the NTK regime with generalization, including label noise and classification.
competitive_landscape.difference: It provides benign-overfitting guarantees under separation conditions rather than attributing a rich-regime deficit to atomic feature representations.

competitive_landscape.title: An Adaptive Tangent Feature Perspective of Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Models feature learning as transformations of tangent features and derives structured, approximately low-rank regularization effects.
competitive_landscape.difference: It supplies an intermediate adaptive-kernel view in place of the reviewed paper's binary lazy-kernel versus atomic-measure comparison.

novelty_assessment: The paper makes a useful counterweight to feature-learning optimism by identifying a concrete representation mismatch: an implicit preference for O(n) atoms can roughen predictions when invariance occupies a continuous family of directions. Its combination of spectral scaling predictions, optimization observations, and image-transformation diagnostics is original. The broad causal story remains a hypothesis because the d>2 exponent is heuristic and the image study does not intervene on sparsity independently of the training regime.
reviewer_notes: Read all 26 extracted pages, including the exact shallow-network objectives, circle proposition and proof, replica/ansatz discussion, training-convergence appendix, image controls, and deformation construction. Competing work was checked on official PMLR and NeurIPS proceedings or arXiv primary pages on 2026-08-23. The review distinguishes the proved two-dimensional statement from the extrapolated high-dimensional exponent and treats the image mechanism as correlational.
